item.title: Holiday 2026 Reading List
item.description: In the bi-weekly PS Book Recommendations newsletter—available for free to all registered PS readers—we highlight insightful, informative, or otherwise compelling books, written or recommended by PS contributors. Here, we present a selection of recent works by PS contributors that are worth adding to your holiday shopping list (and your bookshelf).

item.title: The Summit of Self-Promotion
item.description: Despite claiming that world history was made in Shenzhen with the US–Russia–China Heads of State Declaration toward Peace, the trilateral summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, and Vladimir Putin was about optics, not substance. One of the many important problems they failed to address was China’s export-led growth.

item.title: Why Nvidia Couldn’t Quit Jensen Huang
item.description: Developing AI requires tremendous coordination across firms and sectors, from the AI labs themselves to energy and computing infrastructure, as well as long-term vision and patience. Whereas much of this coordination and planning is led by the government in China, in the US, it has been driven largely by one CEO.

item.title: Chips Too Big to Fail
item.description: The Trump administration pushed for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as CEO of Nvidia to keep the stock market high, to feed a possible productivity surge, and to advance a US foreign policy built on reconciliation with China. But will Americans continue to believe in the AI miracle and this new version of Chimerica?

item.title: Amplifying the Voice of Human Limits
item.description: Tech leaders like Elon Musk have embraced Prometheus as a symbol of creation, conquest, and discovery. But the Promethean impulse must be balanced by the “Orphic” tradition’s respect for and contemplation of nature’s mystery.

item.title: Making the Most of South Korea’s Semiconductor Boom
item.description: The AI boom has driven South Korea’s economic growth well above expectations, thanks to soaring demand for advanced semiconductors. But AI’s transformative potential does not guarantee that the current investment frenzy will continue, leaving the economy vulnerable to a downturn.

item.title: Is a Financial-Market Reckoning Imminent?
item.description: After a year of unprecedented AI investment, increasingly financed by debt in opaque private markets, growing unease about the industry’s future is reflected in sharp declines in the NASDAQ index and the S&P 500. But the stock market’s dependence on a handful of highly leveraged companies—and even a single CEO—is hardly the only source of global financial risk. Amid mounting fears, we asked PS contributors what to expect from financial markets in the year ahead.

item.title: The African Union’s Elusive Quest for Security
item.description: The African Union has long sought to implement Ali Mazrui’s concept of Pax Africana, but has faced persistent logistical and financial constraints. The key to making peacekeeping operations more effective is establishing a better division of labor between the AU, the United Nations, and regional African organizations.

item.title: The Achilles’ Heel of Emerging Economies’ Trade
item.description: New research shows that 23% of global goods imports in 2024 faced at least two of three vulnerabilities: product criticality, supply concentration, and geopolitical distance. Given the wide range of problems, early diagnosis and targeted action are particularly important for emerging economies with limited fiscal space.

item.title: AI Agents Could Make Big Tech Bigger
item.description: The rise of agentic AI could give a handful of Big Tech firms unprecedented power over our personal lives. Unless lawmakers and regulators act now, these digital gatekeepers could manipulate consumers, turbocharge corporate surveillance, and threaten our individual rights and civil liberties.

item.title: If the AI Bubble Is Bursting, the Fallout Will Be Severe
item.description: With the S&P 500 following the tech-heavy NASDAQ into correction territory, even as Anthropic set a record with its initial public offering, this is a good moment to compare AI stock valuations with earlier asset-price bubbles. A look back at the dot-com boom and bust of the late 1990s offers ample cause for concern.

item.title: Journalism Can Be More Than AI Fodder
item.description: As AI fundamentally alters the information environment, news publishers risk becoming little more than content suppliers for Big Tech. To avoid that fate, many are drawing on their archives and expertise to develop AI tools that allow them to operate and compete on their own terms.

item.title: Governing African Economies as They Are
item.description: Africa cannot overcome its development challenges by applying the same knowledge, economic, and innovation systems that helped create them. Imagining and governing new ways forward will require three intellectual ruptures.

item.title: Making Earth Cool Again
item.description: Climate multilateralism is evolving into a two-tiered system in which high-level negotiations toward shared commitments and the real-world implementation of climate solutions become more mutually supportive. Only by unleashing such virtuous cycles can we keep the 1.5ºC target for global warming within reach.

item.title: America’s Lame-Duck Autocrat
item.description: When autocrats suffer a defeat, they tend to double down, such as by intensifying repression at home or behaving more recklessly abroad. With two years left in office after historic midterm election losses, this is the road US President Donald Trump appears to be taking.

item.title: Getting Ukraine’s House in Order
item.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly opposed the idea of forming a national unity government. But bringing opposition leaders into the cabinet would ensure the checks on corruption and wayward bureaucratic action that Zelensky’s team can no longer provide.

item.title: What Adam Smith Missed
item.description: For all that he got right, the "founding father" of economics failed to see how technological innovations lead to market monopolization. If AI is left to the invisible hand, it will almost certainly increase economic and political inequality, causing even deeper social polarization and further undermining democracy.

item.title: China Ratchets Up Its Weaponization of Trade
item.description: Just as the US has been leveraging its large market and technological leadership for geopolitical ends, China is now using its dominance in critical minerals, industrial inputs, and specialized manufacturing machinery to coerce and punish other countries. The consequences, both economic and geopolitical, are far-reaching.

item.title: There Is Only One Thing to Talk About With Russia
item.description: The European security order’s foundational principle is never to tolerate aggression. There is no need to revise that order, as the Kremlin has proposed, only to wait for a Russian regime that is willing to respect other countries’ territorial integrity and uphold its own previous commitments.

item.title: The Truth About Global AI Governance
item.description: Because the current approach to global AI governance presumes that developing countries are full of eager adopters of AI who need to be cautioned about the technology's risks, it overlooks what their information environments and media markets actually need. A survey of researchers who study 71 countries sets the record straight.
